title: Slide 1 · From a score to a range of possibilities
question: Why is 55 not the same as P(pass)?
answer: 55 is a predicted score in points. A pass probability is a number from 0 to 1. To calculate it, specify a passing threshold and the distribution of scores around 55.

title: Slide 2 · What can we already do with tensors?
question: What does the first axis of X count?
answer: The first axis counts examples. In the Study Coach matrix each row belongs to one student.

title: Slide 3 · A prediction is not a promise
question: What additional question can a distribution answer?
answer: For example, it can answer “How likely is Ava to score above 60?” by giving the area above 60 under the score density.

title: Slide 4 · A second question about Ava
question: If Ava's score is 55, must every equally active student score 55?
answer: No. Students with the same recorded inputs can have different outcomes. The model assigns them the same predicted mean.

title: Slide 5 · What is uncertain?
question: What does Y represent before the exam?
answer: Y represents Ava’s exam score before its value is known. After the exam, y denotes the score we observed.

title: Slide 6 · Outcomes and sample space
question: Would Ω change if exam scores include decimals?
answer: Yes. If we record to tenths, Ω includes values such as 67.4. If we model scores as continuously measured, Ω can contain every value in an interval.

title: Slide 7 · Events answer questions
question: Is Y=67 an outcome or an event?
answer: 67 is a possible score. The statement “Y = 67” defines the event containing outcomes that produce that score.

title: Slide 8 · Observed frequency vs model probability
question: What might change if we sampled a different class?
answer: The fraction who pass can change. Even two samples from the same population can contain different numbers of passing students.

title: Slide 9 · Write the first random variable in PyTorch
question: Why is σ not implied by the prediction 55?
answer: 55 locates the center. It gives no measure of spread. We must assume σ or estimate it from observed variation around predictions.

title: Slide 10 · How can a distribution answer a question?
question: Which probabilities must add to one?
answer: Probabilities for a complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1. For pass/fail, P(pass) + P(fail) = 1.

title: Slide 11 · Discrete outcomes: a pass/fail coach
question: If p=0.7, what is P(Y=0)?
answer: P(Y = 0) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. The two outcomes exhaust the possibilities.

title: Slide 12 · Continuous outcomes need density
question: Why does P(Y=55)=0 for an ideal continuous model?
answer: A single point has zero width, so its area under a continuous density is zero, even when the density height there is positive.

title: Slide 13 · Areas answer interval questions
question: Which area corresponds to scores above 60?
answer: Use the area under the density to the right of 60. Each small interval there contributes to P(Y > 60).

title: Slide 14 · The cumulative distribution function
question: How would you use F(60) to compute passing above 60?
answer: F(60) is P(Y ≤ 60). Subtract it from 1 to get P(Y > 60).

title: Slide 15 · Ask PyTorch for the probability
question: Would this tail probability increase or decrease as σ grows?
answer: It increases for this threshold above the fixed mean of 55. As σ grows, 60 lies fewer standard deviations above the mean, leaving more area to its right.

title: Slide 16 · Averages are useful—but incomplete
question: What information is lost when we report only the average?
answer: The average hides how far scores spread and how the distribution is shaped. Classes with identical means can have very different chances of exceeding 60.

title: Slide 17 · Expected value is probability-weighted
question: Compute E[Y] if 50% score 40 and 50% score 60.

title: Slide 18 · Variance measures squared spread
question: Why would using raw deviations give zero?
answer: Signed deviations from the mean cancel. For example, 40 and 60 deviate from 50 by −10 and +10. Squaring makes both contributions positive.

title: Slide 19 · Standard deviation returns to score units
question: Compare two models with σ=5 and σ=15.
answer: With the same mean, σ = 15 has three times the standard deviation and nine times the variance of σ = 5. Its scores spread farther from the mean.

title: Slide 20 · Same mean; different uncertainty
question: Which model predicts scores between 50 and 60 more confidently?
answer: The σ = 5 model puts more probability between 50 and 60. Around a mean of 55, this interval spans ±1 standard deviation for σ = 5 and only ±⅓ for σ = 15.

title: Slide 21 · Sampling approximates expectation
question: Why is n=5 generally less stable than n=1000?
answer: An unusual draw has more influence in a five-draw average. For independent draws with common variance, the standard error of the mean is σ/√n.

title: Slide 22 · One table, three probability questions
question: Which denominator changes if we condition on practice?
answer: Conditioning on at least three practice sets restricts the reference group to the 45 students in that row. The denominator changes from 100 to 45.

title: Slide 23 · Calculate a joint probability
question: What does the number 36 count?
answer: 36 students both completed at least three sets and passed. The joint probability is 36/100 = 0.36.

title: Slide 24 · Calculate the marginal
question: What is P(Practice≥3)?
answer: Add the two cells in the high-practice row. P(practice ≥ 3) = (36 + 9)/100 = 0.45.

title: Slide 25 · Now condition on observed evidence
question: Why is 36/100 wrong for this question?
answer: 36/100 describes the joint event in the entire class. Among the 45 high-practice students, the fraction who passed is 36/45 = 0.80.

title: Slide 26 · Do not reverse a conditional
question: Which denominator describes students who passed?
answer: Start with the 58 students who passed (36 + 22). Among them, 36 practiced at least three sets, giving 36/58 ≈ 0.621.

title: Slide 27 · Test an independence claim
question: Does this association alone show practice causes passing?
answer: No. For instance, prior preparation might influence both practice habits and exam performance. The table alone cannot isolate the effect of practice.

title: Slide 28 · A new practice-test result arrives
question: Should evidence be ignored once we have an initial prediction?
answer: Use the new test result to update the prior. A signal more common among passing students increases the pass probability.

title: Slide 29 · A likelihood describes evidence
question: Why is P(Strong|Pass) not P(Pass|Strong)?
answer: P(Strong | Pass) starts with passing students. P(Pass | Strong) starts with all students who received a strong result. Their denominators differ.

title: Slide 30 · Build the evidence denominator
question: Why must we include the failing group?
answer: Some students who fail also produce a strong signal. Their contribution, 0.25 × 0.40, must be included in the total probability of that signal.

title: Slide 31 · Compute the posterior
question: What if the signal were equally likely in both groups?
answer: For a signal with the same positive likelihood in both groups, the posterior equals the prior. The signal gives no reason to prefer either group.

title: Slide 32 · Weak evidence can reverse the direction
question: Compare the two posterior probabilities.
answer: A strong result raises the pass probability from 60% to about 82.8%. A weak result lowers it to about 28.6%.

title: Slide 33 · Implement a Bayes update with tensors
question: Which tensor operation makes probabilities sum to one?
answer: Multiply prior and likelihood elementwise, then divide by the sum of the resulting weights. The normalized entries sum to 1.

title: Slide 34 · Choose the model from the outcome
question: Can a Gaussian represent exact pass/fail labels without a link?
answer: Use a Bernoulli model for a single pass/fail label. A Gaussian assigns density across a continuum and gives zero probability to either exact point.

title: Slide 35 · Bernoulli: one yes/no result
question: What is the expected value of a Bernoulli variable?
answer: For a 0/1 variable, E[Y] = 1 × p + 0 × (1 − p) = p.

title: Slide 36 · Binomial: how many successes?
question: Why are 10 separate students different from 10 score categories?
answer: Ten students give ten trials whose successes we can count. Ten categories give ten alternatives for one observation.

title: Slide 37 · Categorical: more than two classes
question: Why must class probabilities sum to 1?
answer: Each observation receives exactly one class. Adding probabilities over all classes therefore gives the probability of any possible class, which is 1.

title: Slide 38 · Gaussian: a numerical measurement
question: What happens if the distribution allows scores above 100?
answer: An ordinary Gaussian gives some probability to impossible scores above 100. Check how large that probability is and use a bounded score model if it matters.

title: Slide 39 · Parameters can be tensors
question: What is the difference between a tensor and a distribution?
answer: A tensor stores numerical values. A distribution uses parameters, often tensors, to define how outcomes vary and to compute probabilities or densities.

title: Slide 40 · Data help choose distribution parameters
question: Which quantities are observed, and which do we estimate?
answer: The five scores (42, 48, 55, 61, 69) are observed. We can estimate the population mean μ and variance σ² from them.

title: Slide 41 · Likelihood evaluates parameter choices
question: Why do parameters change while data stay fixed?
answer: The scores have already been observed. Likelihood asks which candidate parameter values assign those same observations greater joint density.

title: Slide 42 · Why take the logarithm?
question: Which operation replaces multiplication?
answer: Taking logarithms turns a product of positive likelihood contributions into a sum of log-likelihood contributions.

title: Slide 43 · Estimate the Gaussian mean and variance
question: Why are there two common variance denominators?
answer: Dividing by n gives the Gaussian maximum-likelihood variance. With an estimated mean and independent, identically distributed observations, dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias in estimating population variance.

title: Slide 44 · Loss is negative log-likelihood
question: What parameters of a Normal model could we learn?
answer: We can learn the mean μ and the positive standard deviation σ. For Ava’s first update we hold σ at 10 and learn the parameters that produce μ.

title: Slide 45 · Fit a distribution in PyTorch
question: Why must σ stay positive?
answer: A Normal distribution requires a positive scale. Zero gives no ordinary Gaussian density, and a negative value cannot represent standard deviation.

title: Slide 46 · Go back to Ava
question: What does the input vector determine?
answer: With fixed weights and bias, the input determines the conditional mean μ(x). Here [2, 3] gives 55. The model specifies σ separately.

title: Slide 47 · Regression: predict a distribution
question: Why is one fixed σ a model choice, not a measured fact?
answer: The mean prediction gives no information about how residuals vary across students. Using the same σ for everyone assumes a common spread.

title: Slide 48 · Classification: output pass probability
question: Why can't we call a raw unbounded score a probability?
answer: A raw score can be negative or exceed 1. A sigmoid maps it into (0, 1), after which we can check how well the resulting probabilities match observed frequencies.

title: Slide 49 · Predictive evaluation asks two questions
question: What happens to log loss when p→0 for a true event?
answer: For an event that occurred, log loss is −log(p). It grows without bound as p approaches zero.

title: Slide 50 · Uncertainty must be supported by evidence
question: When should the coach avoid giving overconfident claims?
answer: For example, if only 60% of students in a held-out group predicted at 90% actually pass, the coach has overstated its confidence in that group.

title: Slide 51 · We have one coherent ML pipeline
question: Which pieces came from Module 1, and which from Module 2?
answer: Module 01 supplied x, w, b and the mean xᵀw + b. Module 02 placed a distribution around that mean and used likelihood to score observed outcomes.

title: Slide 53 · From probability to calculus
question: If the mean moved from 55 to 56, would the density at 60 rise or fall? What would happen to the loss?
answer: The density at 60 rises because 56 is closer to 60 with the same spread. The squared-residual term falls from 25/200 to 16/200, so NLL falls from 3.346524 to 3.301524.

title: Office hours · Why is the predicted score 55 not the student's actual exam score?
question: Why is the predicted score 55 not the student's actual exam score?
answer: The value 55 comes from multiplying Ava's observed features [2,3] by illustrative weights [10,5] and adding bias 20. It is one numerical output from a toy rule. An eventual score can differ because the recorded inputs do not describe every influence. Probability lets us represent plausible outcomes instead of treating a point estimate as guaranteed.

title: Office hours · What is a random variable?
question: What is a random variable?
answer: A random variable assigns a numerical value to each possible outcome of an uncertain experiment. Before the assessment, Y may represent Ava's eventual score. Once the outcome is observed, that realization is an ordinary known number.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between an outcome and an event?
question: What is the difference between an outcome and an event?
answer: An outcome names one possible result, such as a score of 67. An event collects outcomes, such as all scores of at least 60. We assign probabilities to events. For a discrete variable, a single value may also define an event.

title: Office hours · How does empirical frequency differ from a model probability?
question: How does empirical frequency differ from a model probability?
answer: Empirical frequency counts observed cases in a dataset. A model probability describes the proposed process that generates outcomes. The frequency can inform the model but depends on sampling, sample size, and whether the data resemble the target population.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between PMF and PDF?
question: What is the difference between PMF and PDF?
answer: A probability mass function assigns probabilities to individual values of a discrete random variable. A probability density function describes a continuous variable; probabilities are areas across intervals, not the density at one exact point.

title: Office hours · What does the CDF tell us?
question: What does the CDF tell us?
answer: The cumulative distribution function F(t) gives the probability that the random variable is at most t. For a continuous score distribution, the probability of exceeding a threshold is 1−F(t).

title: Office hours · Is the value of a PDF at 55 the probability of scoring exactly 55?
question: Is the value of a PDF at 55 the probability of scoring exactly 55?
answer: No. For an ideal continuous distribution, the probability of any one exact value is zero. The PDF height measures density. Probabilities come from intervals; real exams may have rounded scores, which can be modeled with discrete bins instead.

title: Office hours · What does expectation mean?
question: What does expectation mean?
answer: Expectation is a probability-weighted average over possible outcomes. It is the center of a distribution in the sense of long-run average under standard assumptions, not a promise about one observation.

title: Office hours · Why square deviations when calculating variance?
question: Why square deviations when calculating variance?
answer: The average signed deviation from the mean is zero, so it would not measure spread. Squaring deviations gives positive contributions; the square root converts variance into a standard deviation expressed in the original units.

title: Office hours · Why does a broader distribution matter if the mean stays 55?
question: Why does a broader distribution matter if the mean stays 55?
answer: A wider distribution places more probability on outcomes far from 55. Thus two models can have the same expected score but give different probability for scoring above 60 or staying close to the mean.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between joint and conditional probability?
question: What is the difference between joint and conditional probability?
answer: Joint probability concerns both events and uses the entire population as reference. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases where the conditioning event occurs. In our toy table, 36/100 describes passing and practicing; 36/45 describes passing among practice-group students.

title: Office hours · Why is P(Pass|Practice) not P(Practice|Pass)?
question: Why is P(Pass|Practice) not P(Practice|Pass)?
answer: The first asks how many practice-group students passed, using all practice-group students as denominator. The second asks how many passing students practiced, using all passing students as denominator. In our example they are 36/45 and 36/58.

title: Office hours · Does association imply that practice causes passing?
question: Does association imply that practice causes passing?
answer: No. Even if P(Pass|Practice) is higher than the overall passing rate, prior preparation, motivation, or other unobserved factors can explain some association. The toy table illustrates conditional probability, not a causal study.

title: Office hours · What is a prior in Bayes' rule?
question: What is a prior in Bayes' rule?
answer: The prior represents our probability for a hypothesis before observing a particular new signal. It may come from previous data or modeling assumptions. Updating the prior with new evidence produces the posterior.

title: Office hours · What is the likelihood in a Bayesian update?
question: What is the likelihood in a Bayesian update?
answer: The likelihood describes how probable the observed evidence is under each proposed hypothesis. It is not the posterior probability of the hypothesis. In our example, a strong test is seen with probability 0.8 when a student passes and 0.25 when they fail.

title: Office hours · Why do we divide by total evidence probability?
question: Why do we divide by total evidence probability?
answer: Multiplying prior and likelihood gives unnormalized weights for each hypothesis. Dividing by their sum makes the resulting posterior probabilities sum to one, producing a valid distribution.

title: Office hours · When should I use Bernoulli rather than a Normal distribution?
question: When should I use Bernoulli rather than a Normal distribution?
answer: Use Bernoulli for one binary outcome, such as pass/fail. Use Normal when a continuous measurement is reasonably described by a bell-shaped model. The support of the variable and assumptions must match the task.

title: Office hours · What is the difference between Bernoulli and Binomial?
question: What is the difference between Bernoulli and Binomial?
answer: Bernoulli represents one binary trial. Binomial counts successes across a fixed number of trials, under assumptions such as independence and the same success probability for each trial.

title: Office hours · Why is a categorical distribution different from a regression score?
question: Why is a categorical distribution different from a regression score?
answer: A categorical model assigns probabilities to a finite set of labels, such as low, medium and high. A regression score is numerical and its order and distance generally matter. The two representations answer different kinds of questions.

title: Office hours · What does likelihood optimize?
question: What does likelihood optimize?
answer: For fixed observed data, likelihood evaluates how different parameter settings explain the observations. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters giving the observed data the largest joint probability or density. If the observations are independent given the parameters, each observation contributes one term to the log-likelihood sum below.

title: Office hours · Why use log-likelihood?
question: Why use log-likelihood?
answer: Many likelihood terms multiplied together can become extremely small. Logarithms turn the product into a sum; because log is increasing, the maximizing parameter choice remains the same.

title: Office hours · Why is the Gaussian MLE variance divided by n?
question: Why is the Gaussian MLE variance divided by n?
answer: Maximizing the Gaussian likelihood for a dataset produces an estimate with denominator n. The familiar unbiased sample variance uses n−1 for an unbiased estimate under independent sampling; the two quantities optimize different objectives.

title: Office hours · Can a point model become a probabilistic predictor?
question: Can a point model become a probabilistic predictor?
answer: Yes. The tensor model can determine a conditional mean μθ(x), and a distribution can describe variation around it. This requires choosing or learning a spread and then checking the resulting probabilities against data.

title: Office hours · Why evaluate calibration as well as accuracy?
question: Why evaluate calibration as well as accuracy?
answer: A predictor can classify many cases correctly yet be overconfident. Calibration asks whether events predicted at about 70% frequency occur about 70% of the time across appropriate groups of held-out predictions.
